analysis.one_liner: Lets foreign ships carry cargo between Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico and the mainland, waiving Jones Act rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee with zero cosponsors at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law says ships carrying goods between U.S. ports — including Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other non-mainland routes — must be built in the U.S., mostly U.S.-owned, and mostly U.S.-crewed, the so-called Jones Act. This bill would waive those rules for cargo ships on those routes, letting cheaper foreign-flag vessels compete. It attaches new conditions: minimum international labor and safety standards for all ships in the trade, environmental compliance, and a requirement that foreign owners name a U.S. agent and follow U.S. tax and environmental laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other non-mainland areas, who pay a shipping premium on nearly everything they buy because the Jones Act restricts competition on those routes. Foreign-flag shipping lines would also gain access to a market currently closed to them.

how_it_helps.text: Exempts foreign-flag freight vessels from Jones Act requirements — U.S.-built, U.S.-owned, U.S.-crewed — for cargo moving in noncontiguous trade between the mainland and places like Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico.
Requires every ship in the coastwise trade, U.S.-documented or not, to meet minimum international labor standards for seafarers and all applicable U.S. and international environmental standards.

Requires foreign owners or operators that irregularly enter the domestic trade to name an agent for legal service, follow U.S. laws including environmental and tax laws, and post records of ownership and trip counts aboard the vessel.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flag shipping companies and U.S. shipyards, whose protected market on noncontiguous routes would open to cheaper foreign competition. U.S. merchant mariners could face job losses on those routes, and the U.S.-built fleet that also serves national sealift needs could shrink.

drawbacks.text: U.S. merchant mariners could lose jobs on noncontiguous routes as cheaper foreign-crewed vessels take cargo, weakening the U.S.-flag fleet that also supports military sealift in emergencies.

The bill lets an employer put crew members under a Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation plan that becomes their 'exclusive' remedy, replacing the injured seaman's existing right to sue the employer for negligence under the Jones Act — a real cut to crew legal rights, even as the bill adds other labor standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico, the benefit is potentially large: shipping costs feed into the price of nearly everything, and opening those routes to foreign competition is aimed squarely at that premium. The costs are real but narrower — displaced U.S. maritime jobs and a smaller U.S.-flag fleet with national-security value. The bill is not a clean repeal; it tries to manage the transition with labor, safety, and environmental conditions, though the exclusive-remedy provision for injured crew cuts against its own worker-protection framing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case introduced the bill on January 13, 2021 and delivered introductory remarks on it the same day.
The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Labor Committee.
On February 4, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation — the last action ever taken on the bill.
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows zero.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S.-flag ocean carriers and U.S. shipyards kept their legally protected, competition-free market on noncontiguous routes, and consumers in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico kept paying the shipping premium the law produces.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Protected U.S. shipping carriers and shipyards

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the only sponsor.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referring the bill to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its initial referral.

against.name: U.S.-flag ocean shipping carriers and U.S. shipyards
against.what_they_did: Longstanding opponents of opening Jones Act routes to foreign-flag competition, whose protected market the bill would have opened.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split was recorded; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: These carriers hold a legally protected monopoly-style position on noncontiguous routes, which lets them charge rates above world-market levels; the bill would have ended that protection, lowering costs for consumers in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico.

The Jones Act requires U.S.-built vessels for domestic routes, guaranteeing shipyards a captive market at prices well above foreign-built equivalents; the exemption would shrink that guaranteed demand.
They would gain access to a U.S. domestic trade currently closed to them, but only by accepting the bill's U.S. labor, environmental, and tax-compliance conditions.

Foreign-crewed competition could cost U.S. seafarers jobs on these routes, though the bill extends international labor-standard protections to all vessels in the trade — while also allowing employers to substitute a workers' compensation plan for the right to sue for negligence.
